title: Preekstof
credit: Passion project for Nieuwe Kerk Utrecht
problem: A church service is an hour of talking with two or three minutes in it that people would love to share. Getting those minutes out means cutting, cropping to vertical, adding Dutch subtitles and writing something to post with it. That’s a lot to ask of a volunteer on a Sunday afternoon, so the clips mostly never got made.
approach:
So I built Preekstof. You give it a recording of the service and it turns a moment into a vertical video for Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts. It transcribes the Dutch, lets you correct the subtitles and highlights them word by word. It keeps the speaker in frame, puts music under the voice, adds a corner logo and an end screen, and drafts the text to post with it. It can also go through a whole service and pick out the moments worth sharing. All of it runs on your own computer. I made the app, its landing page and the film that goes with it.

Only the sermon ever leaves the laptop. A rule-based labeller marks the welcome, songs, readings and notices, about half of a Sunday service, and those never go anywhere. The whole service is transcribed once, fast and rough, with Whisper small; only the fragments someone picks are heard again, carefully, with medium. That takes seconds instead of an hour. Claude proposes the moments, and code checks every one: snapped to sentence boundaries, dropped if shorter than 25 seconds or longer than three minutes, flagged if the first line leans on what came before.

The camera in a church is a wide shot from the back, so the app has a camera operator of its own. Two small models on the CPU find the speaker’s face and body, and a motion model moves the crop the way someone on a fluid head would. Most of it is about not moving: a speaker who stands still gets a still frame. The preview in the browser and the final FFmpeg render are the same rules written twice, in TypeScript and in Python, and a mirror test fails the build if they ever disagree. There are about 1,100 tests, and a release only goes out once all six downloads have been installed, started and made to render a clip.
outcome: From sermon to reel, now being piloted by my church
lesson: The people using it aren’t developers. So with every decision I asked myself whether a volunteer could do this without me standing next to them. That’s a higher bar than ‘it works’, and it’s the reason there’s a readiness panel and a one-click start.

title: Virtuele Brigade
credit: For the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee, via Rebels
problem: I joined a training simulation that had been in the works for years. My job was to add multiplayer and VR to it. Quite a task.
approach:
A lot of careful surgery later, instructors can run a scenario together in VR, on a desktop or straight from the editor. I did the development, a great deal of refactoring and the UX flow of the whole application. It gets wheeled out at events, and it’s going to replace the software that new KMar recruits are trained with now. I’m pretty proud of that.

The networking that was there had been a prototype, and it wasn’t built for what was coming. I took it out and designed it again: host-authoritative on Netcode for GameObjects, for sessions an instructor leads over the local network. Joining takes no setup. The lobby finds the host over UDP, and a connection is only approved with the right token and the same build.

Crowds and traffic were too much for that, so they got a UDP snapshot protocol of my own: 32 bytes per NPC, twenty times a second, without allocating memory, with packets split to fit the network and a client that heals itself after a lost one and smooths the movement from a ring buffer. A scenario is a graph of nodes, and it stays in step because the host writes a log of what has been completed and the clients replay it, with checks for drift and for a player’s input racing the host. Scenarios that instructors write themselves travel as a versioned binary package, packed and unpacked on background threads and sent in paced chunks, so the frame rate in VR holds.

I made the architecture abstract enough that the other developers can build on it without knowing networking, and wrote the documentation and failure guides for whoever takes it over.
outcome: Multiplayer VR, retrofitted into a long-running project
lesson: Adding something to a system that already exists is often harder than starting from scratch. These days, before I build a feature, I ask whether anyone is going to maintain it.

title: Alliander HoloLens suite
problem: Alliander has to put transformer houses where nobody wants one. People don’t like an ugly box in their view and they complain, but the energy transition has to start somewhere. The locations were being chosen from paper plans, and we thought that could be done better.
approach:
We tied RTK GPS, an Android phone, a HoloLens and a backend together, so a specialist could stand in the street and see the transformer house in exactly the right spot, to the centimetre. What they saw could be saved and looked at again later, and it gave an idea of the result straight away. I did the development and the UX flow of the application.

The position comes from an RTK tracker, and that was the easy part. Its signal can’t reach the HoloLens directly, so a dedicated Android phone runs an app of ours that passes it on. Then the two have to be lined up: you record where you’re standing, walk five steps forward and record again, which gives the headset its heading as well as its place.
outcome: A transformer house in the right spot, to the centimetre
lesson: Technically it did what it should, and I’m still impressed we got it to work. In practice a HoloLens is a lot of hassle for a field crew. The calibration alone asked a lot of people who weren’t technical and hadn’t wanted the thing in the first place, and it never caught on. Next time I’d push harder for an iPad.

title: Alliander digital twin
problem: Engineers kept driving out to the same sites to check the measurements and sizing of a transformer house.
approach: I built a web tool that puts laser scans, 360° photos and models of the equipment in one place. They could walk around the site from their desk and try things out before anyone got in a van.
outcome: Site visits you can do from your chair
lesson: It worked well, but using it meant changing how people did their job, and the organisation wasn’t ready for that. It was never really adopted.

title: ARCam
problem: Niantic wanted to give visitors a photo with their favourite characters. Think Pokémon, Monster Hunter beasts, basketball stars and the Niantic mascot. It had to work first time, on a busy show floor, in a different city every other week.
approach:
So at Wonderment I built ARCam, an AR photo installation. An iPad running the Lightship SDK puts the characters in the scene, and you look at them through a viewfinder. We made three: one sturdy pedestal and two tripod rigs you can carry. You can take a photo with the characters, which is what everyone came for, or pan around and spot things placed out in the real world.

Behind it sat a backend on Firebase: storage for the files and a database for everything that belonged to them. A photo had to finish uploading before we could show its QR code, which led to a page with a download button. Video was harder, because it went through a few processing steps first. The pedestal itself is all mechanical, so there was nothing in it that software could break. The fiddly part in each new city was the hotspots: look at the Eiffel Tower through ARCam and it tells you about it. All of that was set up in Google Sheets, and today I’d pick something sturdier.
outcome: 16 cities worldwide, and it all fits in a suitcase
lesson: With AR on location you end up owning everything, because the real world is the one part you can’t control. Tracking, databases, web, audio, performance, devices, UX, 3D, and yes, the electronics and the broken screws. I built the backend on a hunch, vibe-coded years before that was a word. It fell over on day one and ran without a hitch after that. Starting on it early, before anyone asked, is what made the difference. And after living out of a suitcase in all those cities, I know what ‘delivering’ means.

title: Wonderment location XR experiments
problem: At Wonderment we kept coming back to one question: what can you build when digital things are pinned to a real place? And could we use that to tell the story of the place you’re standing in?
approach: So we built a run of prototypes that tie AR to GPS and map coordinates, and took them outside to see how they behaved away from a tidy desk. The one I’m proudest of is my own concept: a tour that takes you through the landings of Operation Market Garden, the Allied attempt to liberate the area where I was born. I really wanted to help tell that story.
outcome: A bunch of location-anchored AR prototypes
lesson: Outside, GPS drifts, places change and people walk through your shot. It goes better when you plan for that from the start than when you hope it won’t happen.

title: DTT Projects
problem: I wanted to work on real projects for big clients, and had no idea how. Then I got an internship at DTT. I soon knew this was the job for me, even on the days it didn’t go well.
approach:
I worked on a bit of everything: educational reading games, iOS optimisation, a VR trip through space and an AR showcase app that let clients see what the technology could do.

The trickiest was the star finder. It ran on an early version of Unity’s job system and ECS, with the sky cut into sectors so that only the stars you could see were drawn, and at first I understood none of it. The star map was calculated properly, so if you flew to Venus and looked up, the sky was slightly different from Earth’s. Looking back, that may have been overkill.

The reading game had to run on an iPhone 6, with less than 1 GB of memory. Every byte went to textures. Atlasing helped, but it wasn’t automatic, and the game kept changing.
outcome: A shelf of shipped apps, and my first go at leading a team
lesson: Everyone is pretending until they figure it out. I got these projects because I was willing to try and stuck with them, and I should keep doing that.

title: Lightship Drive
problem: The brief was multiplayer AR on a trade-show floor. That’s about the hardest place there is for a demo: the connection is bad, it’s loud, and nobody has held the app before.
approach:
So we made it a racing game on a table, something you get in five seconds. People race little AR cars across a real table, with spectator screens, synced audio and a server keeping everyone in the same race. The track changes every 30 seconds, and the cars play a kind of tag: whoever is in the lead wears a crown, and the others can take it.

We tried meshing the table first, and it wasn’t accurate enough: the cars bumped into the tiniest dents in the surface. With a track that keeps changing we needed something we could count on, so the whole table became one big tracking image, with a print that’s easy to recognise and not symmetrical. Any iPad that sees it knows where it is. They found each other through a relay that Niantic ran, a new feature they wanted to show off. The rest was Netcode for GameObjects: network variables for the state of the level, RPCs for the collisions.
outcome: AR races on a show floor (and they actually worked)
lesson: On a show floor things fail, so I build as if they will. This time the server SDK was brand new and ended every session after about ten minutes. There was no fix coming, so I added a popup for when it happened: ‘You won! Give the phone to the next visitor.’

title: Zwijsen AR books
problem: Publisher Zwijsen had a new edition of a classic children’s book coming out. They wanted an app to go with it, one that brought the book to life.
approach:
I did all of it: the concept, the UX, the AR and the fiddly business of getting it into the app stores. It went well enough that we did six more books, and then a series of audiobook apps that open from a QR code printed in the book.

It had to work for small children, so there’s nothing to press and no tricky movement to learn. When the camera sees a page, it starts, and the voice and the sounds around it fade in. Most of the work was cutting the pictures out of the pages. I did all of it by hand, and it took weeks of late nights.
outcome: The apps ended up on tens of thousands of phones
lesson: When you make something on your own from start to finish, you find out that the last 10% is most of the work. Support, store reviews, and customer feedback I’d never have thought of.

title: Popcore games
problem: Hyper-casual games live on speed. Ship fast, see how it does, kill it if it flops and start the next one. Everyone is looking for the next hit, and so were we.
approach:
I built new games and added to the ones that were already big, like Parking Jam and Pull the Pin: new modes, multiplayer features, and tools for the level and game designers.

Everything in a game ran on ECS: the gameplay, and even the UI plugged into it. Our games were full of entities (puzzle pieces, tiles, blocks to break, cars to release) and had to run on as many phones as possible, so it made sense. The price was code generation. Every system we added had to be generated with Roslyn, which kept the boilerplate out of sight. A necessary evil, and I had it on a hotkey.

Towards the end of a game the design team came in to make the icons, wallpapers and videos, while QA tested the gameplay. That’s most of why a launch went smoothly.
outcome: Lots of tiny games, shipped fast
lesson: Shipping fast and fixing it afterwards beats elegant code. The market really doesn’t care how pretty your architecture is.

title: Philips medical XR & AI
problem: At Philips we asked whether XR and AI are of real use in a hospital. Or whether we were making cool demos and calling it research.
approach: I worked on a few answers. We improved the VR demos of medical equipment and ran experiments on the Vision Pro. The biggest was a synthetic-data project: digital humans in Unreal, made to train AI that can read a heartbeat from plain video.
outcome: Research that ended up being used in hospitals
lesson: A good part of research is finding out what you shouldn’t build. ‘This isn’t worth it’ is a useful result too, and it’s cheaper in week two than in month six.

title: Amsterdam AI guides
problem: I wanted to know if an AI tour guide could feel like a real person. So I made up a few Amsterdam locals you could talk to, and tried to make them feel less like a chatbot.
approach: The prototype strings together speech-to-text, an LLM, text-to-speech and facial animation. What you get is a character standing in front of you in AR that you can have a conversation with.
outcome: AI locals you can actually chat with in the city
lesson: It worked, and I made the tutorials and the documentation to go with it. It still didn’t do what we’d hoped, and it ended up on the shelf. You can automate the human out of a city tour, but I’m no longer sure you should.

title: Custom AR framework
problem: Before AR Foundation existed, ARKit and ARCore were two separate worlds. If you wanted AR on both iPhone and Android, you built and maintained everything twice.
approach:
For my graduation, at DTT and together with a teammate, I built a framework that put both behind one API. Every AR feature is a subsystem behind an interface (session, camera, planes, point cloud, hit testing, anchors), with an ARKit and an ARCore version of each and a factory that picks the right one for the device. The game code never knows which phone it’s on, and one config asset holds the settings for both.

For multiplayer it used Google’s cloud anchors, so an Android phone and an iPhone could share the same AR scene. The anchor IDs went round through a Firebase realtime database. I’d choose differently today, but it worked for demonstrations. It had 128 unit tests, and it took two ARCore updates by swapping the plugin and nothing else.
outcome: Two AR platforms working together in one tidy API
lesson: Sometimes the tool underneath is worth more than the one problem you built it for. I’ve kept an eye out for that ever since.

title: Kastwezens
problem: Festivals are full of things to look at and short on things to make. We wanted something where a visitor’s own drawing becomes part of the world around them.
approach: We spent a weekend in the woods hanging colourful cabinets between the trees. You draw a butterfly, scan it, and a few seconds later it’s projected onto the forest, flying from cabinet to cabinet. Under the hood it’s Arduino, Unity, webcams, computer vision and projection mapping, but nobody needs to know that. What we were after is the moment someone says, ‘Wait, that’s my butterfly.’
outcome: Draw a butterfly, watch it fly off
lesson: Afterwards nobody talked about the webcams, the UV mapping or the projectors. They talked about the butterfly they’d drawn and watched disappear into the trees. I’d like to make more things that work like that.

title: Land of the Midnight Sun
problem: A student project in Oulu, Finland, with one rule we set ourselves: tell the story without a single line of dialogue. Players had to get it from the world, the mood and what they did in it.
approach: I led the team. We made a third-person adventure in which you guide a young girl through the northern wilderness, with an owl to help her. Besides leading, I built the systems the game runs on, brought in the audio through FMOD, kept the performance up and set up the animation workflow.
outcome: A wordless adventure from Sámi mythology, and first place that year
lesson: This is where I first noticed that every technical choice ends up on screen, in what the player feels. We won first place, which was nice. What stuck with me more was getting programmers, artists and designers to pull in the same direction.

title: Sol.AR
problem: Space is hard to picture because everything in it is too big. A textbook can tell you Saturn has rings, but that’s not the same as standing in them. I wanted space to feel like somewhere you could go.
approach: With ARCore I turned a room into a small solar system. You walk around the planets, look at them up close and pick up facts along the way. If one catches your eye you can go down to its surface, visit the Mars rovers or float around the International Space Station. It isn’t accurate to the millimetre. I wanted it to make people as curious about space as I am.
outcome: The solar system in your living room
lesson: I learn best by walking around something, and I think most people do. AR is good at turning an abstract idea into a thing in your room. Standing in Saturn’s rings sticks better than reading that it has them.

title: Amsterdam Underground
credit: For the Municipality of Amsterdam, via Rebels
problem:
The Municipality of Amsterdam had a VR game about everything that lies under the city’s streets. It was built as a student project, and a good one. Years later it no longer ran on current hardware, and I was asked to update it for an event.

An hour after opening the project I knew an update wasn’t going to do it. The game was made to show an idea, not to be worked on for years. The networking ran through every part of the gameplay, the dependencies were out of date, and getting it to compile meant upgrading half the stack. It needed a rebuild.
approach:
I spent the first two days just reading. For every scene, button and multiplayer interaction I asked whether it still needed to be there. Once I understood how it all fitted together, I rebuilt the networking on Photon Fusion 2, moved the game to standalone Quest headsets and brought the rendering, shaders, haptics and audio up to date.

I left alone what wasn’t broken. The gameplay had rough edges and the balance could have been better, but that wasn’t why it had stopped working. The idea was to keep the same game going for another ten years.
outcome: An old multiplayer VR game, running again on today’s headsets
lesson: With an old project, choosing what to fix matters more than how well you fix it. I found plenty I wanted to improve, and I left most of it alone. That was the hard part.

title: Nieuwe Kerk Utrecht
credit: Passion project for Nieuwe Kerk Utrecht
problem: A few months after joining Nieuwe Kerk Utrecht, I noticed the flyers and posters no longer matched the people inside. I offered to design some new flags and thought that would be it. It wasn’t. The next question was how to make people feel welcome before they’ve even walked through the door.
approach: The flags turned into flyers, posters, stickers, banners, social media posts, PowerPoint slides and visuals for the church’s app. The hard part each time was working out what the thing was for: who would see it, and what they should feel or do next. I started out designing the way I design apps. Over time the style became more the church’s own and less mine.
outcome: New flags for my church, and then everything else
lesson: The better I know who something is for, the better it turns out. Seeing my work printed large and hanging in the church is a good feeling, because it’s a practical way to help. I also found my limit: a full rebrand is a different trade, and it isn’t mine.

title: Eyereader 4D
credit: Student project at Saxion, for the library of Enschede
problem: At Saxion we got the assignment to make an interactive installation for the library of Enschede. We came up with the Eyereader 4D: a ‘4D’ reading experience, where you feel what you’re reading.
approach: We were a team of six, and I took on the technical side. An eye tracker tells Unity where you’re looking while the pages of a book from the library scroll up the screen. When you look at a word I’d marked, Unity sends a message to an Arduino to switch something on: a fan for wind, LED lights for thunder or a lamp, a vibration plate for earthquakes and gunshots, a heater for fire, and a water vapour dispenser for rain.
outcome: A library book that blows wind in your face

title: LED table
problem: Alklima sells Mitsubishi climate installations that run fully on electricity, and wanted to show that off at a convention. The idea was a table with a scale model of a city on it that lights up.
approach: I built the installation that lights it, with LED strips running from building to building. The table has four sectors: retail, living, working and hotels. An Arduino lights the strips in order, and when a sector is fully lit it tells a second Arduino to light that sector’s symbol on the panel behind the table. The software is C++. The hard part was doing several things at the same time on a board that isn’t built for it, and FreeRTOS got that working.
outcome: A scale-model city, lit up one sector at a time
